newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Prices, weak won hit 1996 net at S.Korea's POSCO.
newsitem.headline: Prices, weak won hit 1996 net at S.Korea's POSCO.

text.p: Falling product prices and currency conversion losses hit earnings at South Korea's largest steelmaker Pohang Iron and Steel (POSCO), but company officials and analysts forecast a better performance this year.

POSCO said on Wednesday its after-tax profit declined to 623.96 billion won ($721.76 million) in calendar 1996 from 839.71 billion a year earlier. Sales amounted to 8.45 trillion won against 8.22 trillion won.
But the world's second-biggest steelmaker forecast 878.7 billion in net profit this year. Nippon Steel Corp is the world's largest in terms of crude output.
"A drop in steel product prices led to slower net profit growth last year," said Oh Dong-ho, an official in POSCO's accounting department.
Analysts said the average sale price on the local market fell five to six percent last year, while that of higher value-added stainless steel declined by 15-20 percent on the year.
They said slower demand, inventory build-ups and shipments from European countries and the United States had forced world steelmakers to lower their prices.
A foreign currency translation loss of 180 billion won was also cited as another factor behind POSCO's profit fall. The won depreciated against the dollar by eight percent last year.
The construction of an additional blast furnace at Kwangyang steel mill raised the depreciation costs eating into POSCO's earnings.
Whang Soo-hyun of Daewoo Securities said rising iron ore and coal prices also depressed profits.
"I believe the worst is over. Prices have hit bottom," POSCO's Oh said.
He added a global economic recovery would improve the steel industry fundamentals and help raise steel prices this year.
Analysts agreed POSCO would experience a better year in 1997 but they remained conservative on its earnings outlook.
"There is no doubt POSCO will post a good rise in profit this year. But it will not be as rosy as the company forcasts," said Anthony Moon of H.G. Asia.
He predicted POSCO's after-tax profit would rise to 780 billion won in 1997. Daewoo's Whang was more optimistic, with a figure of around 800 billion.
Kwangyang mill's depreciation cost was completed last year, and Moon said this would contribute to a jump in POSCO's profit this year.
Kim Dong-jun of Ssangyong Securities was more pessimistic, forcasting net profit at 570 billion won.

"Demand for steel products is expected to rise by only 3.5 percent, but world production will increase too," Kim said. "Uncertainty over foreign currency fluctuations will also act as negative factors for POSCO."
POSCO relies on imports for its raw materials and pays for these in dollars, making for higher bills due to the depreciation of the won.
"On the other hand, POSCO exports most of its goods to Japan which pays in yen. The won is appreciating against the yen," Kim said.
Analysts said their POSCO earnings forecasts did not include the impact of the company's purchase of Sammi Steel Co's stainless steel operation.
In February POSCO took over Sammi's Changwon plant and the rights to its steel pipe and bar technology for a total of 719.4 billion won.
"This will eventually help POSCO lower its production costs. But who can guess what the short-term financial burden will be," said Daewoo's Whang.
(Conversion $1 = 864.50)
